content: Schistosomiasis is an infection caused by contact with freshwater contaminated with the infectious larval form of Schistosoma flatworms (trematodes). While it is primarily a tropical disease, it can affect travelers, students, immigrants, veterans, and tourists who have lived in or visited endemic regions. Early stages of the disease are often asymptomatic unless Katayama fever, an acute immune complex disease, develops. In its later stages, schistosomiasis becomes symptomatic and can manifest as hepatosplenic schistosomiasis (pre-sinusoidal portal hypertension), urinary and urogenital schistosomiasis (urinary obstruction, genital symptoms), schistosomal glomerulopathy (chronic immune complex deposition in the kidneys), or ectopic disease affecting the lungs and central nervous system (CNS). Diagnosis involves identifying Schistosoma eggs in stool, urine, or biopsy tissues, as well as serologic assays and urinary antigen testing. Ultrasound imaging may reveal characteristic scarring patterns in hepatosplenic and urogenital disease. Praziquantel is the first-line treatment for schistosomiasis. Historically, schistosomiasis has been referred to as bilharzia or bilharziosis, named after Theodor Bilharz, the German physician who first described the cause of urinary schistosomiasis in 1851. The full disease cycle was later described by Pirajá da Silva in 1908. Schistosomiasis was a significant cause of death in ancient Egyptian populations during the Greco-Roman period. Schistosomiasis can be classified based on organ involvement into intestinal and urogenital forms. The pathogenesis of acute schistosomiasis is primarily driven by egg deposition and the release of antigens from adult worms and eggs. This triggers a strong inflammatory response characterized by elevated levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines, such as interleukins 1 and 6, tumor necrosis factor-alpha, and circulating immune complexes. The life cycle of schistosomes involves both vertebrate and invertebrate hosts, with humans serving as the definitive host. Infection occurs when cercariae penetrate human skin or through contact with contaminated soil. The incubation period for acute schistosomiasis ranges from 14 to 84 days. Both early and late manifestations of the disease are mediated by the immune system. Chronic schistosomiasis is associated with egg retention in host tissues, leading to chronic granulomatous injury. Schistosomiasis is caused by Schistosoma species, including S. intercalatum and S. haematobium. It must be differentiated from other parasitic infections, such as tapeworm infections (e.g., diphyllobothriasis, hymenolepiasis, and taeniasis), which can also cause abdominal pain, fever, chills, cough, and muscle aches. Globally, over 600 million people are exposed to Schistosoma parasites, with 200 million infected and 20 million symptomatic cases reported. All age groups are susceptible, but school-aged children and adolescents in endemic areas have the highest disease intensity. There is no racial predilection, and the disease affects men and women equally. The primary risk factor for schistosomiasis is skin exposure to contaminated freshwater, such as during wading, swimming, washing, or working in infested water. Travel to endemic areas is another risk factor. Routine screening for schistosomiasis is not recommended for travelers but may be used to guide mass public health treatment programs in endemic villages. If left untreated, schistosomiasis can progress to complications such as bladder, liver, or kidney cancer, as well as kidney failure. Common complications include hematuria, malnutrition, intestinal polyps, hydronephrosis, glomerulonephritis, bladder polyps, bladder cancer, infertility, ectopic pregnancy, renal failure, and cor pulmonale. Prognosis depends on the extent of disease progression at diagnosis but is generally favorable with treatment. In the early phase, most patients are asymptomatic unless Katayama fever occurs. Late-stage schistosomiasis presents with hepatosplenic disease (pre-sinusoidal portal hypertension), urinary and urogenital disease (urinary obstruction, genital symptoms), schistosomal glomerulopathy (chronic immune complex deposition in the kidneys), and ectopic disease in the lungs or CNS. Physical examination findings may include generalized lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, rash, fever, right upper quadrant tenderness, urticaria, and bloody stool. Diagnostic methods include identifying Schistosoma eggs in stool, urine, or biopsy tissues, serologic assays, and urinary antigen testing. Laboratory findings may reveal circulating antibodies to schistosomes and schistosomal antigens in serum. Chest X-rays may show patchy infiltrates, increased vascular and interstitial markings, and mild lymphadenopathy in pulmonary schistosomiasis. CT scans can detect nodular and ring-enhancing lesions with surrounding edema in neuro-schistosomiasis, calcified capsules in hepatosplenic disease, and interstitial fibrosis in pulmonary schistosomiasis. Ultrasound findings may include bladder wall scarring in urogenital schistosomiasis and periportal fibrosis in intestinal schistosomiasis. There are no specific findings on MRI or ECG for schistosomiasis. The primary treatment for schistosomiasis is pharmacotherapy, with praziquantel being the drug of choice. Corticosteroids may be added for patients with neuro-schistosomiasis or severe Katayama fever. The goals of treatment are to eradicate the helminth and address any complications of infection. While praziquantel is safe and effective, it does not prevent reinfection and is not an optimal solution for individuals living in endemic areas. Surgical intervention is rarely recommended but may be necessary to manage complications such as esophageal varices or genitourinary granulomatous masses. Primary prevention measures include avoiding swimming or wading in potentially infested freshwater, boiling water for bathing to kill cercariae, and vigorous towel drying after accidental water exposure. Secondary prevention measures are similar to primary prevention strategies.
